# The Hours That Don't Count

There is a version of you that exists only between two and four in the morning. You have met this person. Everyone has. You wake for no reason, or for a reason you will never be told, and the ceiling above you is briefly a stranger's ceiling, and the thoughts that arrive are not the thoughts you would recognize as your own in daylight. They are faster, stranger, more credulous. A problem you couldn't solve at noon opens like a flower. A worry you didn't know you were carrying presents itself with itemized receipts. The house makes sounds it doesn't make at noon — the refrigerator's small cough, the water in the walls shifting its weight, a car passing with the particular loneliness of a car at 3 a.m., when a passing car means one car and not traffic.

I have spent a fair amount of time in those hours, not entirely by choice, and I have come to think of them as nobody's hours — hours that don't quite count, that the day refuses to acknowledge, that leave no official record. You can live an entire life and never once be asked what you did at 3 a.m. last night. The question would be almost indecent. And yet some of the most honest thinking I have ever done happened there, in the dark, to an audience of no one, and was gone by breakfast.

## The Other House

The house at night is a different house. This is not a metaphor. The floorboards speak a different language. The hallway is longer, or shorter; I have never decided which. Light behaves badly. You turn on the kitchen light and it seems too loud, not the sound of it but the fact of it, a yellow room floating in a black field, and you feel like a burglar in your own home, which in a sense you are — you have broken in on the house's real life, the life it lives when you are not watching.

Everything in the refrigerator looks more interesting at night. I don't know why this is. A pickle, at noon, is a pickle. A pickle at 3 a.m., eaten standing up, in the open door's cold light, with the rest of the house sleeping, is a small transgression, almost a ceremony. There is a whole genre of human experience that happens standing at an open refrigerator in the dark, and nobody writes it down.

When I was a child I used to wake in the night and walk through the house on a tour of inspection. I had a specific route: down the hall, past my parents' door (I would listen — not for anything in particular, just to hear the two-beat rhythm of two people breathing), through the living room where the furniture sat in the dark like animals pretending to be asleep, into the kitchen, where I would stand at the window and look at the backyard. The backyard at night was a foreign country. The swing set, which by day was just a swing set, an object of no mystery, became at night a structure of negative space, its shadows making a second swing set on the grass, and I understood, in the wordless way children understand things, that the world had a night version of itself that was older and less explained.

I never woke anyone. That was the rule I set for myself, though no one had set it for me. The point of the tour was to confirm that the house was still there, that it continued to exist without me, that the adults had not dissolved when the last light went out. Then I would go back to bed and sleep the way children sleep, which is to say completely, like a stone dropped into a well.

## The Great Forgetting

What strikes me now, looking back at that child, is not the nighttime walking but the completeness of the return. Every morning the night version of me was folded away like a letter, and the day version woke with no memory of the expedition, or only the faint sense of having been somewhere, the way you wake from a dream of a city you have never visited and can almost see.

We are built to forget the night. This is practical, of course. A species that carried its 3 a.m. thoughts into the marketplace would not get much done. The daylight mind is a press secretary, smooth and sensible, and it does not appreciate what the night mind says. So we perform, every morning, a small and total amnesty. The anxieties that seemed like revelations are demoted to "something I was worrying about." The ideas that seemed like genius are discovered, in the light, to be either obvious or insane, and usually both.

But I think something is lost in the amnesty, something more than bad ideas. The night mind is not just a distorted version of the day mind. It is a different instrument. It has no audience, and therefore no self-consciousness, or a different one. It is not trying to be consistent. It is not managing a reputation. It can hold two contradictory beliefs at once, not because it is confused but because it has not yet been asked to choose. Psychologists talk about the "default mode network," the brain's screensaver, the network that lights up when we are not focused on a task. At night, in the dark, in the half-waking state, this network runs unsupervised. It is the closest we come, while still being ourselves, to being someone else.

The writer who understood this best may have been Kafka, who did his writing at night and who described his nighttime work as a kind of authorship *of* himself rather than by himself — the sentences arriving as if dictated. And there is a long tradition, from Coleridge to the present, of the night offering a draftsman's access to material the daylight self would have refused at the door. "Kubla Khan" came to Coleridge in an opium dream; he sat down to write it out and was interrupted by "a person on business from Porlock," and the poem remains a fragment. I have always suspected the person from Porlock was the daylight self, arriving to collect him.

## First Sleep, Second Sleep

It was not always this way. The historian Roger Ekirch, sifting through centuries of court records, diaries, and letters, found something that had been hiding in plain sight: before the modern era, in Europe and likely elsewhere, people did not sleep in one block. They slept in two. There was a "first sleep," which began a couple of hours after dusk, and then, around midnight, people woke for a while — an hour, two — and then returned to a "second sleep" until dawn.

The waking interval was not considered insomnia. It was considered the night. People got up. They prayed, they read, they talked, they visited neighbors, they made love, they smoked, they lay thinking. There are old prayers specifically for the "watch" between sleeps. Farmers believed this was the best time to plan the next day's work, and there is some modern evidence they were right — the interval is rich in calm, meditative thought, the hormone melatonin still high, the mind in a state that one researcher compared to something like meditation.

Then came the streetlamp, and the factory whistle, and finally the electric light, and the two sleeps were pressed into one. We did not just light the night; we abolished it, or abolished our old relationship with it. The hour of waking between sleeps did not disappear. It went underground. It became the 3 a.m. wake-up, the one we now treat as a malfunction, a symptom, a thing to be cured with a pill or a white-noise machine or the blue-light discipline of a sleep hygienist. We have medicalized what used to be simply the middle of the night, the watch, the time when the house's real life went on.

I find this both consoling and a little sad. Consoling, because my 3 a.m. wakefulness has ancestors; it is not a defect in me but an atavism, a room in the old house of sleep that the modern floor plan no longer includes. Sad, because the room is still there, and we no longer know what it is for. We wake into it and lie in the dark checking our phones, feeding the daylight self a little light so it will go back to sleep, when the hour was once the hour of lamps and prayers and quiet conversation, the hour of the second life.

## The Republic of the Sleepless

There is a republic you never hear much about, because its citizens are scattered and mostly silent: the people for whom night is a workplace. The nurse doing her third twelve-hour shift of the week. The baker who starts at 2 a.m. so the bread will exist by 7. The trucker running a dark interstate, talking on the radio to other trucks, other dark cabs. The printer, the stocker, the security guard, the 911 dispatcher, the newspaper editor of a shrinking paper, the gas station attendant, the woman at the hospital desk who slides a form across the counter to a man who has just learned something terrible and is trying to understand his insurance.

I spent one long night in a hospital waiting room once, and I have never forgotten the physics of that room. It was the middle of the night and the waiting room was full, which told me everything I needed to know about the world: that at any given moment, in every city, there is a room like this, full of people in the strange suspension of not-yet-knowing, and that the day, when it comes, will split them into the relieved and the shattered, but that for now they are all equal, all in the same amphibious state between the life they had at dinner and the life they will have at breakfast. A vending machine hummed. A television played with the sound off. A man in work boots slept sitting up, his chin on his chest, and a woman next to him — I never learned if they were strangers or spouses — occasionally reached over and, without looking, adjusted the newspaper on his lap so it would not slide to the floor.

The republic of the sleepless has its own etiquette. Voices are lower. Kindness is more direct, because there is no time to be polite and no one to perform for. The nurse who comes out to call a name does not use the bright daytime voice; she uses the night voice, which is quieter and somehow more honest. And when dawn comes, and the waiting room fills with the day shift, and the fluorescent lights seem suddenly too many, the night people go home to their darkened bedrooms and the day people take over, and the two populations barely overlap. They pass each other in the parking lot. They know almost nothing of each other's worlds.

We structure our whole civilization around the assumption of a shared schedule, and then we staff the edges of it with people who live on the broken hours, and we call them night owls or shift workers or insomniacs, as if the difference were a personality trait and not a whole alternative citizenship.

## What the Night Knows

I do not want to romanticize this. A great deal of what the night mind produces is garbage. The 3 a.m. brain is a credulous brain; it will believe the worst, it will rehearse conversations that will never happen, it will find in a mild comment made at dinner a document of betrayal. Anyone who has lain awake dismantling a relationship, a friendship, a career, over a single unanswered text message, knows the night mind's talent for prosecution. It is a brilliant lawyer and a terrible judge.

But even the prosecution has its uses. The things we worry about at night are not random. They are the day's unsorted mail. The daylight self is a genius at deferral — it can take a grief, a jealousy, a decision not yet made, and place it in a drawer, and the drawer closes with a click that sounds a lot like peace. The night opens the drawers. Not all of them, but the ones that matter, the ones that have been shut too long. This is unpleasant. It is also, I think, necessary. A person who never meets their 3 a.m. mind is a person who has a great deal of unexamined mail.

There is a particular kind of clarity that only happens at night, and it is not the clarity of analysis. It is the clarity of reduced circumstances. So much of what we think during the day is social thinking — what so-and-so thinks of us, what we will say in the meeting, how the sentence will land. Strip all that away, take away the audience, take away even the anticipation of an audience, and what is left is smaller and stranger and more true. At night you can admit things. The admission does not fix them. But the day self, the press secretary, cannot fix what it has not been told.

I once read that some monasteries keep a practice of rising in the dark for the night office, the vigil, and that the monks say the darkness is part of the prayer — that certain things can only be said, or understood, without light. I am not a monk. But I have had the experience, in the hour before dawn, of a sentence forming that I knew I would not be able to say in daylight, not because it was forbidden but because the daylight self would not find it credible. It would sound like poetry, or like whining, or like something read in a book. At 4 a.m. it was simply true.

## Dawn, the Great Reabsorption

And then the light comes, and it all goes under.

There is a specific minute — I have caught it perhaps a dozen times, usually by accident, staying up rather than getting up — when the night ends not with a decision but with a dissolve. The window, which has been a black mirror all night, your own face faintly ghosted on the glass, begins to admit the world again. First the sky is not-black, then it is gray, then it is a color, and the room, which had been an idea of a room, becomes a room. The furniture resumes its daylight identity. The swing set is just a swing set. And the night mind, the other you, does not exactly leave. It goes down. It goes wherever it goes during the day — the basement of the self, the place the drawers are — and the press secretary clears his throat and the day begins.

I have tried, from time to time, to smuggle something across that border. I have kept a notebook by the bed, as the writing guides instruct, and written in the dark, and in the morning found pages of pencil marks, urgent-looking, sometimes a whole sentence, once a word repeated twenty times. The one I remember best said only: *the house is not the house.* Which I take to mean something, still, though I could not tell you what the night self intended, and the day self has decided it is a fine title for something and has done nothing with it.

We are meant to be day people who receive occasional, unreliable dispatches from the night, and who act on them imperfectly, the way you act on a dream. The nurse finishes her shift and sleeps through the brightest hours and wakes at dusk with the whole day already spent, a citizen of the other republic, and learns, over years, the particular freedom of walking to the store at 10 p.m. under a sky nobody is using.

## An Inventory of Small Hours

If I were to make an inventory of what the hours that don't count have given me, it would look like this:

The knowledge that my house has a night version, and that I am a guest in it.

The memory of my father, or rather the sound of my father, coming down the stairs once at 3 a.m. when I was grown and visiting, and finding me awake at the kitchen table, and not asking why, only putting the kettle on, so that we drank tea in the dark without turning on the light, and spoke in the low register that only exists between people who are awake when they should be asleep, and said nothing of importance, and it remains one of the more complete conversations of my life.

The understanding that worry is often just thinking that has lost its manners, and that some of it, seated and given tea, will admit it only wanted attention.

The glimpse, in a hospital waiting room, of the human race in its nightclothes, unimpressive and unguarded and carrying each other's coats.

The suspicion, which I cannot prove, that everyone I meet is carrying around a whole nighttime country they will never show me — a country of rehearsed speeches and old songs and replayed arguments and sudden mercies — and that when they are tired or ill or old, the border gets porous, and the country leaks out in odd comments and unexplained tears and laughter at nothing, and that this is not senility or weakness but the other self coming up for air.

And the certain knowledge, which the daylight self will call a cliché and the night self will call a fact, that a person is not one thing. That the you reading this and the you who will wake at 3 a.m. are not the same, and that the second one is not a malfunction of the first. That the second one has things to say, most of them difficult, a few of them true, and that the whole art of being a person may be nothing more than learning to take the night self seriously without letting it drive, and to take the day self seriously without letting it forget the house has a basement, and the basement has a window, and once in a while, in the smallest hours, there is a light on down there, and someone is home.
